about1: I build with AI: agents, automations, web projects and games.
about2: My first web page went online in May 2026. Since then I have published two multiplayer browser games, both of which connect players directly through PeerJS instead of a game server, and Nivra, an organizer that keeps its data on your own device.
about3: The games run in the browser and are free to open. They, this site and Wii Party Recomp are open source on GitHub.
about4: Since September 2026 I have also been working on Wii Party Recomp, which translates a Wii game into C++ so it runs natively on PC.
candyAlt: A 6 by 6 board of colored candy tiles while a player chooses where to hide the poison.
candyBuilt1: Plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript, with no framework and no build step. It opens straight from index.html.
candyLead: A multiplayer board game for 2 to 5 players. Find the poisoned candy before it finds you.
candyModes1: Locally, 2 to 5 players share one device and pass it around. Online, a room gets its own code and players connect peer-to-peer through PeerJS, with no game server.
candyModes2: Every room can be set up before starting: board size from 2 to 10 rows and columns, wildcards and stock per player, time to act and to pick poison, poisoned candy per player, starting lives, the candy skin, and a random-wildcards mode without the shop.
candyRound1: Each round, every player secretly chooses which tiles hold poisoned candy. Then they take turns eating from the board. Eat a poisoned one and you lose a life. Whoever is left standing with the most lives when the match ends wins.
candyShop1: Before each round there is a shop. Players pick wildcards with special effects, like vision, protection or forced moves, from a limited stock per match. There are fifteen of them, in five groups: protective, attack, information, interaction and strategic.
candyShopAlt: The wildcard shop, with fifteen wildcards grouped as protective, attack, information, interaction and strategic.
candySummary: A board game for 2 to 5 players. Everyone hides poisoned candy on the board, then takes turns eating. Pass one phone around, or play online in a room with a code.
colophon: Set in Cormorant Garamond, Lora and Geist. Built with Astro, without JavaScript in the browser.
helloDesc: My first web page, from May 2026.
heroIntro: I build web projects and games with AI, from Spain.
metaDescription: Arel Kair builds web projects and games with AI: Wii Party Recomp, Nivra, Pool and Poisoned Candy.
nivraAlt: The Nivra dashboard in dark mode, with the sidebar sections and today's date as the heading.
nivraInstall1: It ships a web app manifest and a service worker, so it can be installed from the browser and opened like any other app.
nivraLead: A private organizer for the browser. Calendar, timetable, tasks and more, stored on your own device.
nivraPhoneAlt: The Nivra welcome screen on a phone, listing calendar, timetable, tasks and private.
nivraPriv1: There is no sign-up. Nivra asks for your name and keeps everything in your browser.
nivraSummary: A private organizer for calendar, timetable, tasks, grades and money. There is no account: everything stays in your browser.
nivraWhat1: Nivra is organized in four groups.
poolAlt: A game of Pool in progress: the green table seen from above, with the shot and potted counters at the top.
poolCode1: The code is split by responsibility. The physics are not a library: collisions, friction and pockets are handled by a billiards engine written for this game, and there is a self-test for it.
poolLead: A 2D pool game for the browser, with online 1v1 multiplayer and a physics engine written for it.
poolModes1: Singleplayer is free practice. Multiplayer is a 1v1 match: one player creates a game and shares a four-letter code, the other joins with it. Turns follow standard 8-ball rules.
poolModes2: To shoot, drag from the cue ball and release. The further you pull, the more power.
poolNet1: The two players connect to each other peer-to-peer through PeerJS. There are no game servers to run and nothing to set up on the router.
poolSummary: A 2D pool game with online 1v1. One player shares a four-letter code, the other joins, and the match runs peer-to-peer with standard 8-ball rules.
stackNote: Only tools used in a published project, and where.
wAudio: The game's recompiled audio microcode and sound output
wCore: Runs the translated code: memory, threads, interrupts and boot
wGpu: Wii graphics commands drawn with Direct3D 11 on Windows and OpenGL on Linux
wInput: An emulated Wii Remote, driven by keyboard, mouse and gamepads
wRecompiler: PowerPC and audio DSP recompilers, written in Python
wiiCopy1: The repository has no Nintendo assets, game code or binaries. You need your own legally obtained copy of Wii Party, and the tools work from a dump of that disc. The project is not affiliated with or endorsed by Nintendo.
wiiEstimate: These percentages are my own estimates, not measurements.
wiiHow1: The project is split into a reusable Wii engine and one folder per game, so other Wii games could be recompiled with the same tools.
wiiHow2: The main executable, about 7,350 functions, and all 115 of the game's modules are translated into C++ and build into a single native program of roughly 440 MB. It runs using about one and a half CPU threads and 200 MB of memory.
wiiLead: A static recompilation of Wii Party for PC. The game runs as a native program on Windows and Linux, with no emulator.
wiiNext2: The code is open source under the GPL, and issues and pull requests are welcome on GitHub.
wiiNow1: The game boots, reaches every menu and has been played through a complete game of Board Game Island: 17 rounds, up to the final ranking and the save. It runs at a steady 60 fps, with sound from the game's own audio microcode and in the language of your system. A launcher that updates itself builds it from your own PAL or NTSC-U disc in about ten minutes, also without an internet connection. The Linux version is new and still experimental.
wiiNow2: Some things are still missing. Every minigame has been played without faults, but the other modes have only been tried, not played through, and pointing with a real Wii Remote and a sensor bar is untested.
wiiSummary: A static recompilation of Wii Party for PC. The game's code is translated into C++ and built as a native program for Windows and Linux, with no emulator.
wiiWhat1: The original game executable is translated into C++ source code that is compiled natively, so the game runs on PC without an emulator. The Wii hardware it expects, from the graphics and audio chips to the Wii Remote, is recreated around that code.
